title: Flying With Thanksgiving Leftovers: What You Can Bring
summary: Learn how to fly with Thanksgiving leftovers, including TSA carry-on rules, food safety tips, packing advice, and international restrictions.
body_markdown:
Thanksgiving leftovers can make the trip home almost as good as the meal itself. Before packing turkey, stuffing, or a slice of pie, check TSA guidelines and food safety recommendations. This guide explains which leftovers can go in your carry-on, which can travel in checked baggage, and how to keep perishable food cold throughout your journey.
‍


## **Can You Bring Thanksgiving Leftovers on a Plane?**


Yes. Most solid foods can travel in either a carry-on or checked bag. Turkey, ham, stuffing, solid casseroles, mac and cheese, pies, cakes, and cookies are generally allowed through airport security.


Foods that can spill, spread, spray, pump, or pour must follow the TSA liquids rule. If gravy, cranberry sauce, soup, jam, or another liquid or gel is larger than 3.4 ounces, pack it in a checked bag. Food may require additional screening, and the final decision rests with the TSA officer at the checkpoint.
‍


## **Thanksgiving Leftovers: Carry-On or Checked Bag?**


Food Carry-On Guidance Checked-Bag Guidance


Turkey, chicken, or ham Allowed when solid Allowed


Stuffing Allowed when solid Allowed


Mac and cheese Allowed when solid Allowed


Casseroles Allowed when solid; liquid or semi-liquid portions must follow the 3.4-ounce rule Allowed


Pies, cakes, cookies, and brownies Allowed Allowed, but protect them from damage


Gravy Limited to containers of 3.4 ounces or less Pack larger amounts in a checked bag


Cranberry sauce Limited to containers of 3.4 ounces or less Pack larger amounts in a checked bag


Soup, sauces, jam, and preserves Limited to containers of 3.4 ounces or less Pack larger amounts in a checked bag


Frozen gel packs Allowed only when frozen solid at screening Allowed


‍


The TSA’s rule is easier to remember than the full list: solid foods can usually go through the checkpoint, while liquids and spreadable foods larger than 3.4 ounces should be checked. If you are unsure about an item, review the latest[TSA Thanksgiving food guidance](https://www.tsa.gov/news/press/releases/2025/11/24/tsa-prepared-busy-thanksgiving-travel-kentucky-offers-special) before packing.
‍


## **Keep Perishable Leftovers Cold**


Airport security rules determine whether food can enter the terminal. Food safety guidance determines whether it will still be safe to eat when you arrive.


According to[USDA food safety guidance](https://www.fsis.usda.gov/food-safety/safe-food-handling-and-preparation/food-safety-basics/how-temperatures-affect-food) , bacteria grow rapidly between 40°F and 140°F. Refrigerate leftovers within two hours of cooking and transport cold food in a cooler with ice or frozen gel packs. If perishable food has been above 40°F for more than two hours—or more than one hour in temperatures above 90°F—it may no longer be safe to eat.


Cool leftovers completely before packing them. Divide large portions into shallow, sealed containers so they chill faster and fit more easily in a cooler or insulated bag. Pack the containers directly from the refrigerator shortly before leaving home.


Use enough frozen gel packs to keep the food cold throughout the drive to the airport, security screening, the flight, baggage claim, and the trip to your final destination. If you cannot keep turkey, stuffing, casseroles, or other perishable dishes at 40°F or below for the full journey, leave them behind.


After arriving, refrigerate the food as soon as possible. When you are ready to eat, the USDA recommends reheating leftovers to 165°F.
‍


## **Make Sure Ice Packs Are Frozen Solid**


[Gel ice packs](https://www.tsa.gov/travel/security-screening/whatcanibring/items/gel-ice-packs) can go through airport security when they are frozen solid. If they are partially melted, slushy, or have liquid at the bottom of the container, they must follow the TSA liquids rule.


Freeze the packs well before your trip and keep the insulated bag closed on the way to the airport. A long drive, warm car, or frequent opening can cause them to thaw before you reach security.


If you plan to use dry ice, check TSA guidance and your airline’s rules before packing. Airlines may set limits on the amount allowed and require specific packaging.
‍


## **Pack Leftovers to Prevent Leaks and Damage**


Use sturdy, leakproof containers with secure lids. Avoid loosely covered serving dishes, foil trays, and glass containers that could break or open in transit.


Pack sauces separately from solid foods. Place each container in a resealable bag as a second layer of protection, then arrange the food so heavier items cannot crush pies, cakes, or other delicate dishes.


Keep carry-on food easy to reach. TSA may ask you to remove food from your bag for additional screening, so avoid burying it under clothing or electronics. Check your airline’s carry-on size and weight rules if you are bringing a cooler or insulated food bag.
‍


## **Should You Carry On or Check Your Leftovers?**


A carry-on gives you more control over how your food is handled and kept cold. It may be the better choice for small portions of turkey, stuffing, baked goods, and other solid foods that fit within your airline’s baggage rules.


A checked bag may be the better option for gravy, cranberry sauce, soup, and other liquid or spreadable foods larger than 3.4 ounces. Seal each container tightly, place it in a second leak-resistant bag, and cushion it inside your luggage.


Remember that checked bags may be exposed to changing temperatures or delayed in transit. Do not rely on cold weather or the aircraft’s cargo hold to keep perishable food safe.
‍


## **Check Rules Before Flying Internationally**


TSA rules apply at U.S. airport security checkpoints, but customs and agriculture rules determine whether food can enter another country or return to the United States.


When entering the United States, travelers must[declare agricultural products](https://www.cbp.gov/travel/clearing-cbp/bringing-agricultural-products-united-states) , including meat, fruits, vegetables, and other plant or animal products. Some foods may be restricted or prohibited based on where they came from. Declaring an item does not guarantee that it will be allowed, but failing to declare can lead to confiscation and penalties.


Check the destination country’s rules before flying with Thanksgiving leftovers internationally. If you are returning to the U.S., declare every food item and let a CBP agriculture specialist determine whether it can enter.


Travelers flying from Hawaii, Puerto Rico, or the U.S. Virgin Islands to the U.S. mainland should also check agriculture restrictions before packing fresh fruit or vegetables.

## **Pack Thanksgiving Leftovers With Confidence**


Most solid Thanksgiving leftovers can fly, but liquid and spreadable foods larger than 3.4 ounces should go in checked baggage. Refrigerate food promptly, pack it with frozen solid ice packs, and keep perishable items at 40°F or below throughout the trip.


Before leaving home, check TSA guidance, your airline’s baggage rules, and any customs or agriculture restrictions that apply to your route. With a little planning, your leftovers can make it home safely and ready to enjoy.
